newsitem.title: UK: Budget, output cuts set to dominate cocoa talks.
newsitem.headline: Budget, output cuts set to dominate cocoa talks.

text.p: The International Cocoa Organisation (ICCO) council meeting in London next week will set output targets needed to balance supply and demand as well as tackle the pressing question of financing the ICCO secretariat.
The September 9-13 council meeting is also expected to examine a possible EU directive on the use of non-cocoa vegetable fats in chocolate-making, delegates said.
The Cocoa Producers Alliance (CPA) of exporting nations met on Friday ahead of the ICCO meeting to map out a common strategy. The ICCO groups 36 producer and consumer nations.
Discussions at the ICCO meeting will centre on the future of the group's production-management plan, designed to help restore market equilibrium and ensure remunerative prices.
The plan has been in tatters after a record harvest by Ivory Coast, the world's top producer.
The ICCO said the meeting will consider "fixing of indicative tonnages of annual cocoa production necessary to achieve and maintain equilibrium between cocoa supply and demand".
At the last meeting in June, the members agreed to introduce a target range of eight percent, instead of a single-point target which has so far been missed.
New production targets will be set next week after an agreement on which level of stock/grinding ratio -- the bellwether of market prices -- to use.

The producers said in June that they were considering a stocks-to-grindings ratio of between 30 and 35 percent. One consumer delegate said a draft secretariat's proposal called for a ratio of between 28 and 32 percent.
In June, the ratio stood at 47.5 percent or five-and-a-half months of world consumption.
Consumers say they would favour a higher ratio as it would help smooth any price rallies.

But no consumer proposals were seen yet and one western delegate said: "It is something that we haven't focused on yet. We will wait and see what the producers say...but it will have to be realistic and workable."
Producer and consumer states will also try to resolve the question of how to continue funding the London-based ICCO secretariat after buffer stock sales run out.
Buffer stock sales now make up around 40 percent of the ICCO's budget of around 2.7 million a year but are due to run out in April 1998.
"We have to find ways to meet this shortfall," one said.

Importing and exporting states are pushing for a 30 percent cut in operational costs and to raise members' contributions by a marginal three percent a year over the remaining three years of the agreement's tenure.
At the same time, they also called for the setting up of a reserve fund of 2.5 million stg to serve as a liquidation fund.
"Surprisingly, producers and consumers are thinking very much along the same line," one conference source said.
The secretariat has instead proposed marginal savings in operational costs, to substantially raise members contribution and establish a reserve fund of 10 million stg.

One delegate said: "The general message is all the same. The most important way of filling these reductions in the budget after 1998 is for the executive director to announce significant cuts and just top it up with the small increase in contributions and money generated from this reserve fund."
